lesson.title: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
lesson.subtitle: From water to Wasser, better to besser, and two to zwei

hook.title: The Sibilant Explosion
hook.content: When ancient Germanic 'T' shifted in High German, it became a hissing sibilant: 'ss' or 's' after vowels, and 'z' (/ts/) at the beginning of words. This single rule instantly unlocks dozens of the most frequent everyday words.

footnotes.title: Spirantization
footnotes.content: Voiceless alveolar stop [t] relaxed into the alveolar fricative [s] or affricate [ts].

pattern.title: T after vowels becomes S / SS
pattern.content: Water becomes Wasser. Eat becomes essen. Better becomes besser. Hate becomes hassen. Out becomes aus. What becomes was. Great becomes groß (think of 'gross income' or 'gross error' = large/total, not yuck!). At word beginnings, English 'TW-' maps to German 'ZW-': two becomes zwei, twig becomes Zweig (a two-fork split), twice becomes zweimal, and twenty becomes zwanzig.

footnotes.title: Street ↔ Straße & Eszett (ß)
footnotes.content: Roman paved roads (via strata) gave English 'street' (keeping Latin 't') and German 'Straße' (shifting 't' to sharp 'ß'). The letter 'ß' represents a sharp [s] sound after long vowels (groß, Straße).

pattern.linguist_note: The German letter 'z' is always pronounced like the 'ts' in English 'cats' or 'tsunami', reflecting the original dental stop that broke into an affricate.

exercises.prompt: Assemble the German word for 'water' (das + stem + ending):

vocab_hints.note: German uses das for neutral gender nouns

exercises.affirmation: You hissed the t into ss and kept the das — the receipt reads water → Wasser.
exercises.explanation: Water: T shifts to SS after short vowel = das Wasser.

exercises.prompt: Match the English T words to their German S/SS/Z shifts:
exercises.meaning: better, to eat, two, to hate
exercises.affirmation: Four t-words hissed into German — ss after vowels, z at the front door. You're starting to hear it everywhere.
exercises.explanation: T becomes ss after vowels, and z at the start of words.

exercises.prompt: What consonant shift connects English 'better' and German 'besser'?
exercises.affirmation: You read besser backwards to better — the doubled ss whispers its tt origin.
exercises.explanation: Medial tt shifted into geminate sibilant ss.

exercises.prompt: What native English word shares the root of 'essen'?
exercises.affirmation: You swapped the ss for a t and eat stepped out — one sibilant, one ancient stem.
exercises.explanation: German 'essen' and English 'eat' are identical Germanic stems with T → SS shift.

exercises.idea: you're at a café counter asking for a drink: a glass of water, please
cues: English t hisses into ss after a vowel: water → Wasser
Measure phrase, no 'of': ein Glas Wasser
Seal it with bitte — the cognate of English 'bid'

vocab_hints.note: cognate with English 'bid' (as in 'I bid you welcome' / 'at his bidding')—literally: '[I] bid/request it'

exercises.explanation: Measure phrase without 'of', the T → SS receipt on Wasser, and bitte to close — your first café order, built from a thought.

summary.outcome: Recognize common t and s/ss/z word connections and order a simple request.
summary.takeaway: English 't' regularly maps to German 'ss', 's', or 'z'.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: the tw → zw openers — zwei, Zwilling, Zwerg: the /ts/ costume party of the z-letter.

twist.prompt: Same order, but you're thirsty times two: a glass of water becomes two glasses of water. (German measure words don't take a plural ending.)
twist.explanation: After a number the measure word stays bare: zwei Glas Wasser — Gläser, the true plural, waits for other jobs. Friction on purpose: this exact slip is common and harmless.

essen.shift_rule: T → S / SS / Z + Ablaut Vowels
essen.context_translation: What do we want to eat?
essen.etymology_derivation: Medial t → ss. Noun: das Essen (food).

aus.context_translation: I come from / out of Berlin.

zu.etymology_derivation: Initial t → z [ts]. Functions as both intensifier (too) and infinitive particle (in order to).

groß.etymology_derivation: T → S/ß shift from Germanic "great". Preserved in English "gross income", "gross national product", and "a gross error" (large, not disgusting).

straße.etymology_derivation: Roman paved road (via strata) gave English "street" (kept Latin "t") and German "Straße" (shifted "t" to sharp "ß").

dreizehn.shift_rule: TH → D + T → S / SS / Z
dreizehn.context_phrase: Mein Sohn ist dreizehn Jahre alt.
dreizehn.context_translation: My son is thirteen years old.
dreizehn.etymology_derivation: drei + zehn — thirteen with a double shift: th → d and t → z. [wiktionary]

fünfzig.context_phrase: Die Frau ist fünfzig Jahre alt.
fünfzig.context_translation: The woman is fifty years old.
fünfzig.etymology_derivation: fünf + -zig — fifty with the same -ty twin suffix and the t → z shift. [wiktionary]

mittagessen.context_phrase: Das Mittagessen ist um zwölf Uhr.
mittagessen.etymology_derivation: Compound of Mittag and Essen; Mittag is literally mid day with the d to t correspondence, and essen corresponds to English eat via the t to ss shift. [wiktionary]

beißen.shift_rule: T → S / SS / Z + Ablaut Vowels
beißen.etymology_derivation: From Old High German bīȥan, from Proto-Germanic *bītaną. English bite is a listed cognate, with the same ablaut as bite bit bitten. [wiktionary]

kalender.context_phrase: Ich schreibe den Termin in meinen Kalender.
kalender.context_translation: I write the appointment in my calendar.
kalender.etymology_derivation: From Latin calendārium — the same Latin word that gives English calendar. [wiktionary]

erdnuss.shift_rule: TH → D + T → S / SS / Z
erdnuss.etymology_derivation: Erde + Nuss, literally earth-nut: Erde is the twin of earth (th to d) and Nuss the twin of nut (t to ss), the same building blocks as the English word earthnut. [wiktionary]

wasserfall.context_phrase: Der Wasserfall fällt in den tiefen See.
wasserfall.context_translation: The waterfall falls into the deep lake.
wasserfall.etymology_derivation: Wasser + Fall — the exact compound calque of waterfall; Wasser carries the sibilant shift (t → ss), Fall is the twin of fall. [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
